title: The fundamental theorem of calculus
keyIdea: The rate the area grows is the height of the curve, so integrating and differentiating undo each other: ∫ₐᵇ f dx = F(b) − F(a).

kid: Imagine painting the area under a curve, moving to the right. How fast does the painted area grow? As fast as the curve is tall.
So the area has gradient f. That means the area is an antiderivative of f. To find an area from a to b, find an antiderivative F and work out F(b) − F(a).
adult: If A(x) = ∫ from a to x of f(t) dt, then A′(x) = f(x): a thin extra strip has area about f(x) × h, so (A(x + h) − A(x))/h → f(x).
Any two antiderivatives differ by a constant, so F(b) − F(a) is the same whichever F you pick; the + C cancels. Differentiation and integration are inverse processes.

familyTip: Fill a tall thin glass and a wide bowl from the same tap. Which water level rises faster? Link the width to how fast the 'area' grows.

practice.prompt: A(x) is the area under f from 0 to x. What is A′(x)?
practice.hint: How fast does the area grow?
practice.explain: The area grows at the rate of the curve's height: A′(x) = f(x).

practice.prompt: F(x) = x² has F′(x) = 2x. Find ∫ from {a} to {b} of 2x dx.
The height of f at x = {x} is {h}. How fast is the area A(x) growing there?
Why does + C not matter in F(b) − F(a)?
practice.explain: The two Cs cancel, leaving F(b) − F(a).

pool.prompt: Which pair of processes undo each other?
pool.explain: Differentiation and integration are inverse processes.

pool.prompt: A(x) = ∫ from 0 to x of (t + {c}) dt. Find A′(4).
pool.hint: A′(x) is the curve's height at x.

pool.prompt: If F′(x) = f(x), which equals ∫ from a to b of f(x) dx?
The area function A(x) grows fastest where…
pool.explain: Its gradient is f(x), so it rises fastest where f is biggest.

visual.caption: Drag the right edge. The area graph (right) rises at a rate equal to the height of f (left).
